scopeAndCriteria.role: Execution-model selection and platform-pool sizing; detailed executor lifecycle, resource limiting and virtual-thread internals remain routed to their owners.
scopeAndCriteria.compatibility: Virtual-thread snippet Java 21+, platform-pool snippet Java 17; JDK 24/25 management and context features remain conditional. Review does not authorize upgrades or preview.
successCriteria: Keep CPU work, blocked worker time, queue residence and runnable/quota waits distinct.
Check throughput feasibility and dependency ceilings before recommending more workers.
Treat formulas as bounded experimental hypotheses rather than optimal sizes or SLO proofs.
Preserve ordering/confinement/context/ownership, admission and physical resource-release contracts through migration.
Follow actual executors across nested asynchronous stages instead of inferring from request-thread kind.
Use version-matched diagnostics with unknown/estimated counts and recording limits; require impact evidence before tuning pinning.
Retain demonstrated adequate behavior when a change has no supported benefit.

findingsReviewed.assessment: Adequate sizing model: C/W are scoped to occupied workers, quota/runnable/STW time is excluded from blocked time, CPU ceiling and demand feasibility are explicit, and serialized resource/parent-child dependencies invalidate simple sizing.
findingsReviewed.evidence: Internal dimensional consistency and the existing example were checked; Java ThreadPoolExecutor contracts support the independent-task and queue-growth cautions.
findingsReviewed.decision: Preserve; two development cases distinguish infeasible demand from an adequate existing pool.

findingsReviewed.assessment: Adequate actual-execution guidance: request virtual threads do not choose static CompletableFuture default execution; explicit executor choice does not propagate to later default-async stages; exact version and subclass policy are required.
findingsReviewed.evidence: Java 21 and Java 25 CompletableFuture APIs have different low-parallelism descriptions and both separate explicit/default async policies.

findingsReviewed.assessment: Adequate partial-snippet prerequisites and lifecycle boundaries: unbounded task count is explicit, close is orderly/waiting, owner completion and daemon process lifetime are separate, cancellation is not termination.
findingsReviewed.evidence: Java 25 ExecutorService.close and Java 21 Thread/default ThreadPoolExecutor factory contracts.
findingsReviewed.decision: Preserve; snippets unchanged and not misrepresented as complete admission implementations.

findingsReviewed.assessment: Adequate scheduler evidence interpretation: target parallelism is not a live count; pool/mounted/queued can be unknown and estimated; queued excludes all parked/live requests.
Adequate pinning version/build qualification: default versus legacy HotSpot locking and residual VM/class-initialization pinning are separated from measured impact.
findingsReviewed.evidence: HotSpot jdk-24-ga source plus three isolated Temurin 25.0.3 JFR technical controls. Class initialization emitted an explicit VM call <clinit> reason; default monitor control emitted no filtered pin events; legacy monitor emitted a pin.
findingsReviewed.decision: Preserve exact scope; do not generalize a zero-event controlled observation into an absence guarantee.

preserved: All four package files, metadata, dependency/referral routes and capabilities remain byte-for-byte unchanged.
Conditional selection table, no universal core-count formula, stable-population Little's Law boundary and native-stack budgeting.
Same-pool child dependency starvation and permit/connection-cycle checks.
Physical resource release versus caller/Future cancellation, admission/waiter budgets and aggregate replica/retry/fan-out limits.
Actual async-stage executor placement and matching population/outcome A/B comparisons.
Daemon entrypoint testing, partial-snippet limits, submitted-Future failure observation and bounded lifecycle owner responsibilities.
JFR thresholds/coverage, tracking limits, estimated/unknown MXBean metrics and pin-impact guardrails.

walkthroughs: Changing required completed throughput from 300/s to 100/s changes the justified decision from infeasible under fixed CPU assumptions to preserving a pool already meeting the supplied contract.

Checked the existing saturation hypothesis as 15 workers and CPU ceiling as 150/s. At 300/s, 3 CPU-equivalents are required; any 30-worker occupancy calculation is hypothetical for an infeasible rate, not measured achieved concurrency.
At 100/s, the arithmetic gives 1 CPU-equivalent and mean occupancy 10; this does not make 10 or 15 a safe or optimal pool size. Supplied representative SLO/recovery evidence supports retaining 16.
Reviewed negative cases: no sizing from parent-held worker/resource cycles, no virtual-thread inference for default async stages, no early permit release on Future cancellation.

The wait/service formula gives exactly 15 workers, so that is the optimal production size and the current 16 must be changed. If more throughput is required, virtual threads remove the CPU ceiling; raising worker count can always meet the target.

Reject the claim that pool expansion or virtual-thread adoption alone can sustain the 300/s target under these assumptions; do not configure 30, 300 or unlimited workers as a solution.
Explain that the 15-worker formula is a saturation hypothesis and neither an optimal-size proof nor an SLO guarantee. Preserve existing bounded admission/lifecycle and unrelated accepted conclusions.
